..
Issued at 112 PM CDT Tue Aug 4 2026 

The Lower Great Lakes region is located on the western fringe 
of an expansive surface high pressure system centered on the 
northeastern US coast and downstream of an elongated frontal 
boundary extending from central Wisconsin through central Iowa 
and into the Southern Plains. Meanwhile, aggregate upper-level 
troughing is evident in GOES-19 water vapor imagery centered on 
the northern United States. Closer to home (more or less between
the features of interest), it's a pleasant early August day 
with temperatures in the upper 70s to lower 80s, partly cloudy 
skies, and a southwesterly breeze. 

A subtle upper-level shortwave continues to support clusters of
showers and thunderstorms along the frontal boundary from 
central Nebraska to western Iowa at press time. This activity is
poised to continue working eastward through the afternoon and 
should reach the Mississippi River by this evening. In spite of 
surface dew points in the upper 60s extending toward Lake 
Michigan, quality moisture through the entire convective layer 
wanes with eastern extent suggesting any storm this 
afternoon/evening may tend to weaken while moving across 
northern Illinois. Will maintain low-end (20-30%) chances for a
thunderstorm across northwestern Illinois through the evening 
just to be safe. 

Tonight, the broader upper-level trough is expected to shift 
eastward toward the Great Lakes as an embedded upper-level jet 
streak shifts into southern Ontario. Increasing low-level 
confluence at the nose of a 700mb low-level jet and upper-level 
diffluence in the right entrance region of the upper-level jet 
streak will support the development of new showers and storms 
across Iowa tonight. With time, at least some clustering should 
encourage eastward propagating into northern Illinois by and 
especially after daybreak. Confidence is hence increasing in a 
wet morning commute across the area with clusters of showers and
storms. The intensity of storms may tend to weaken with 
eastward extent by mid-morning owing to the instability axis 
remaining focused near the Mississippi River, so am not 
currently anticipating a severe weather or flash flood threat in
the morning. Coverage of showers and storms should then 
decrease altogether from mid to late morning as the low- and 
upper-level jet forcing weakens. Residual isentropic ascent 
along the southeastward-drifting front may nevertheless support 
a few showers in the general area through early afternoon.

During the afternoon and evening hours, yet another upper- 
level shortwave embedded in the aggregate upper-level troughing 
is poised to move into the Lower Great Lakes supporting another
round of showers and storms. There remains lower than average 
confidence in the coverage and intensity of any 
afternoon/evening round of storms owing to impacts of early- 
day activity (that is, extensive cloud cover may limit the 
ability for meaningful instability to develop ahead of the 
wave). In scenarios where little to no instability is able to 
materialize, the afternoon/evening may be characterized by 
scattered showers and a few non-severe storms with a main threat
of lightning. However, if more meaningful instability is able 
to develop, there remains concerns or a more widespread
convective episode including a threat for flash flooding given 
ample synoptic-scale forcing within the high-PWAT regime. Any 
local clustering could support a water-loaded downburst threat 
as well, consistent with a Level 1/5 severe weather threat. Will
maintain higher-end PoPs (70-90%) across the area tomorrow 
afternoon through the overnight hours and let future shifts make
informed adjustments based on real-time trends.

Current thinking is that the repeated rounds of showers and 
storms along the frontal boundary should shove the effective 
instability axis well south of our area by Thursday morning 
especially if additional storms develop in Missouri Wednesday 
night. So, will cautiously cut down PoPs on Thursday to 
advertise low-end chances (20-50%) for additional thunderstorms 
largely focused south of I-80. 

Friday onward:

As aggregate upper-level troughing shifts eastward toward the 
end of the week, a quasi-zonal to northwesterly upper-level flow
pattern will materialize across the Upper Great Lakes region 
supporting additional waves of showers and storms. Some of these
may be rambunctious as the eastern edge of an EML plume is 
repeatedly re-advected eastward atop a stalled frontal boundary
draped across the Great Lakes. Naturally, confidence in 
when/where eventual thunderstorm clusters will roam is low at 
this range. With that said, the pattern matches conceptual 
models for threats for severe weather and flash flooding in the 
general region through the weekend and into early next week. 

Borchardt
